name: slots.courseSpecifics
description: The students are Norwegian upper-secondary students in Vg2 who have chosen English 1 as a programme subject after compulsory English in Vg1. English is their second language and most have Norwegian as their first. Work in English at an advanced, academic level, and when an error comes from Norwegian (word order, articles, prepositions, false friends), name the contrast with Norwegian briefly. Practice texts should be set in, or be about, the English-speaking world. The course gives one written and one oral grade for coursework, and a student can be drawn for a centrally set written exam of five hours with no preparation day, or for a locally set oral exam.

name: Reading strategies
description:
Skimming: reading quickly for the gist and the main points.
Scanning: searching a text for one particular piece of information.
Close reading: reading slowly to understand details, language and argument.

name: Choose a reading strategy for the purpose
description: choose a reading strategy that fits the purpose, such as skimming a long report to judge whether it is relevant and then reading the relevant section closely, and switch strategy when the purpose changes.

name: Take notes from a talk or podcast
description: take structured notes from an English lecture, podcast or documentary, listening for the overall message as well as for figures, names and reasons, and use the notes to retell the content.

name: Write in stages
description: plan, draft, revise and proofread a text in separate stages, fixing content, structure and argument before correcting language.

name: Keep a demanding conversation going
description: keep a demanding conversation going by paraphrasing, asking for clarification, checking that you have been understood and rephrasing when you have not, instead of switching to Norwegian.

name: Work systematically on your own errors
description: find your own recurring errors in feedback on earlier texts, and choose a strategy for each, such as a personal checklist or targeted practice.

name: Use translation tools and AI to learn
description: use translation tools and AI chatbots to learn rather than to write for you: ask for explanations of your errors, check their suggestions against a dictionary or grammar, and keep the text your own.

name: Comma splice, run-on and fragment
description:
Comma splice: two main clauses joined with only a comma, as in "The report was clear, it was too long."
Run-on sentence: two main clauses run together with no punctuation or linking word.
Sentence fragment: part of a sentence written as if it were complete, as in "Because the costs rose."

name: Fix comma splices and fragments
description: find and fix comma splices, run-on sentences and fragments in your own text, choosing between a full stop, a semicolon, a linking word and a subordinate clause.

name: Vary sentence length and structure
description: vary sentence length and structure in a text: join short sentences with subordinate clauses, split overloaded ones, and open some sentences with something other than the subject.

name: Passive and nominalisation
description:
Passive voice: a structure where the thing acted upon becomes the subject, as in "The law was passed in 2010", so that the doer can be left out.
Nominalisation: turning a verb or adjective into a noun, such as decide into decision, which makes a text more compact and formal.

name: Use the passive and nominalisation with judgement
description: use the passive and nominalisation where they suit a formal text, and rewrite with active verbs where they make a sentence heavy or hide who did what.

name: Keep tenses under control in a long text
description: keep tenses consistent through a longer text, choose correctly between the present perfect and the past simple, and use the present tense when writing about what happens in a literary work.

name: Make the verb agree in hard cases
description: make the verb agree with the subject in difficult cases: a long subject, "one of the", "there is" and "there are", collective nouns, and uncountable nouns such as information, research and evidence.

name: Use articles with general and abstract nouns
description: decide when to use the and when to leave it out with general and abstract nouns, such as society, nature, history, the environment and the government.

name: Revise your own text for language
description: revise your own text at word, sentence and text level, using what you know about vocabulary, sentence structure and linking to make it clearer and more precise.

name: Register
description: Register: the level of formality in speech or writing, from formal (academic texts, official letters) through neutral to informal (chat, talk among friends), shown in word choice, contractions and sentence structure.

name: Adapt the register
description: adapt word choice, contractions and sentence structure to the purpose, audience and situation, and rewrite a text from an informal to a formal register or the other way round.

name: Academic vocabulary and subject-specific terms
description:
Academic vocabulary: words used across many subjects in academic texts, such as analyse, significant, consequence, whereas and approach.
Subject-specific term: a word with a precise meaning in one field, such as inflation in economics or natural selection in biology.

name: Write precisely with academic vocabulary
description: replace vague everyday words such as thing, get, big and a lot of with precise, academic alternatives, without making the text stiff.

name: Use and explain subject-specific terms
description: use the subject-specific terms of a topic you have worked on correctly, and explain them for a reader who does not know the field.

name: Collocations and phrasal verbs
description:
Collocation: words that are normally used together, such as make a decision, play a role and raise awareness.
Phrasal verb: a verb and a particle that together have their own meaning, such as carry out or put off.

name: Use natural collocations
description: use natural collocations instead of word-for-word translations from Norwegian, such as make a mistake rather than do a mistake, and prefer a one-word verb to a phrasal verb in formal writing.

name: Choose the right form in a word family
description: choose the right word from a word family, such as economy, economic, economical and economist, using prefixes and suffixes to tell word class and meaning.

name: Commonly confused words in formal writing
description:
affect: to influence (verb)
effect: a result (noun)
economic: to do with the economy
economical: saving money or resources
principle: a basic rule or belief
principal: main, or the head of a school
imply: suggest without saying directly
infer: conclude from what is suggested
fewer: used with countable nouns (fewer people)
less: used with uncountable nouns (less time)
historic: important in history
historical: to do with the past
complement: something that completes or goes well with something else
compliment: praise

name: Hedging
description: Hedging: softening a claim to show how certain you are, with words such as may, seems, likely, tends to and to some extent.

name: Match your claims to your evidence
description: state a claim as strongly as the evidence allows, using hedging where it is uncertain and avoiding sweeping words such as always, everyone and never.

name: Linking words
description: Linking word: a word or phrase that shows how ideas relate, such as addition (furthermore), contrast (however, whereas), concession (although, admittedly), cause and effect (therefore, as a result), example (for instance) and conclusion (in conclusion).

name: Cohesion and coherence
description:
Cohesion: the links between sentences, made with linking words, reference words such as this and these, repetition and synonyms.
Coherence: the logical order of ideas, so that the reader can follow the thread through the whole text.

name: Bind a text together
description: bind sentences and paragraphs together with varied linking words and clear reference words, and put a noun after this or these when the reference would otherwise be unclear.

name: Types of factual text
description:
News report: a text that tells what has happened, most important facts first.
Feature article: a longer, more personal text that explores a topic in depth.
Opinion piece: a text that argues for the writer's view, such as an editorial or a column.
Report: an organised account of an investigation, usually with headings.

name: Identify purpose, audience and text type
description: identify the purpose, intended audience and text type of a factual text, and explain how they shape its language and structure.

name: Summarise a long factual text
description: summarise a long factual text in your own words, keeping the main argument and leaving out examples and details.

name: Explicit and implicit information
description:
Explicit information: what a text states directly.
Implicit information: what a text suggests without stating it, which the reader infers from word choice, selection and tone.

name: Read between the lines
description: work out a writer's implicit attitudes and assumptions from word choice and from what is included and left out, and support your reading with quotations.

name: Rhetorical appeals
description:
Ethos: persuading through the speaker's credibility and character.
Pathos: persuading by stirring the audience's emotions.
Logos: persuading through facts, reasoning and logic.
Kairos: saying the right thing at the right moment and in a way that fits the situation.

name: Analyse a persuasive text
description: analyse how a speech or opinion piece tries to persuade, through the appeals and devices such as repetition, rhetorical questions and contrast, and assess how well it works.

name: Read a text from another subject
description: read an English text from another subject, such as a popular science article on climate, health or technology, and explain its main points and key terms to a reader without the background.

name: Describe a graph or table
description: describe and interpret a graph, table or chart in English, with precise language for trends such as rise steadily, level off, peak and fall sharply, and say what the data do not show.

name: Research article
description:
Research article: an academic text reporting a study, usually with an abstract, an introduction, a method section, results, a discussion and a reference list.
Abstract: a short summary at the start of a research article.

name: Find the essentials in a research article
description: find the research question, method and main finding of a research article by reading the abstract, the headings and the discussion first.

name: Reflect academically on a text
description: reflect on a text academically: relate it to other texts and to what you know, weigh its claims, and say what it adds to your understanding of the topic.

name: Source criticism
description: Source criticism: evaluating a source by asking who made it, for what purpose and audience, when, what evidence it builds on, and whether independent sources confirm it.

name: Search for sources effectively
description: search for English sources with precise keywords, quotation marks and filters, use search tools for academic texts such as Google Scholar, and change the search when the results are poor.

name: Assess a source
description: assess how reliable and relevant a source is for your purpose, and explain your judgement with reference to sender, purpose, date and evidence.

name: Bias and misinformation
description:
Bias: a one-sided presentation that favours one view, often without saying so.
Misinformation: false information spread by people who believe it is true.
Disinformation: false information spread on purpose to mislead.

name: Detect bias in a source
description: spot bias in a source through word choice, the facts selected, framing and images, and compare it with a source that has a different slant.

name: Check a claim across sources
description: check a claim by leaving the page and finding out what independent sources say about the claim and about whoever made it.

name: Quotation, paraphrase and summary
description:
Quotation: a source's exact words, in quotation marks.
Paraphrase: a source's point in your own words, about as long as the original.
Summary: the main points of a source in your own words, much shorter than the original.

name: Work sources into your own text
description: work quotations and paraphrases into your own sentences with signal phrases such as according to and X argues that, and comment on each one instead of letting it stand alone.

name: In-text citation and reference list
description:
In-text citation: a short reference in the text to where an idea or quotation comes from, such as (Smith, 2023).
Reference list: the full list of sources at the end of a text, in alphabetical order.
Citation style: a fixed system for references, such as APA or MLA.

name: Cite sources consistently
description: cite sources in the text and list them in a reference list, following one citation style consistently.

name: Plagiarism
description: Plagiarism: presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own, including text produced by an AI tool or a source used without a reference.

name: Task words
description:
discuss: weigh arguments for and against and reach a conclusion
analyse: break something into its parts and show how they work and why
compare: point out similarities and differences
explain: make clear how or why something is as it is
reflect: consider something from several angles and show your own thinking
assess: judge the value, importance or effect of something, with reasons
present: give an organised account of something
elaborate: develop a point further with details and examples

name: Answer exactly what the task asks
description: read a writing task closely, identify the task words, the topic and any required sources or text type, and plan a text that answers exactly what is asked.

name: Essay structure
description:
Introduction: the opening paragraph, which leads into the topic and states the thesis.
Thesis statement: one or two sentences in the introduction that state the main claim or angle of the text.
Body paragraph: a paragraph that develops one point, opening with a topic sentence.
Conclusion: the closing paragraph, which draws the argument together.

name: Write a thesis statement
description: write a thesis statement that is specific and arguable, and keep the rest of the text tied to it.

name: Write a well-built paragraph
description: write a paragraph that develops one point: a clear topic sentence, explanation, evidence or examples, and a sentence linking it back to the thesis.

name: Write the introduction and conclusion
description: write an introduction that leads into the topic and states the thesis, and a conclusion that draws the argument together without just repeating it or adding new points.

name: Types of essay
description:
Argumentative essay: an essay that argues for one position.
Discussion essay: an essay that weighs several views before reaching a balanced conclusion.
Analytical essay: an essay that examines how a text or phenomenon works and why.

name: Write an argumentative essay
description: write an argumentative essay that builds a position with evidence and answers the strongest counterargument.

name: Write a discussion essay
description: write a discussion essay that presents several views fairly, weighs them against each other, and reaches a conclusion that follows from the discussion.

name: Write an analytical essay
description: write an analytical essay about a text, organised by points of analysis rather than by retelling the text, with quotations as evidence.

name: Write a feature article or formal letter
description: write a feature article, blog post or formal letter for a defined audience and purpose, with a fitting title, opening and register.

name: Write a long text from sources in limited time
description: plan, write and revise a long text that answers a task within a fixed time, using given sources critically and accountably.

name: Word stress
description: Word stress: the syllable spoken louder and longer in a word; within a word family the stress can move, as in PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy and photoGRAPHic.

name: Pronounce academic English clearly
description: speak clearly with correct word stress on academic words such as analysis, develop and economy, and keep to one accent consistently.

name: Give an academic presentation
description: give a structured presentation on an academic topic, with a clear main point, signposting between the parts and a conclusion, speaking from keywords rather than a script.

name: Take part in a formal discussion
description: take part in a formal discussion: build on what others say, disagree politely with reasons, and ask follow-up questions that move the discussion on.

name: Formal debate
description:
Motion: the statement a debate is about.
Proposition: the side arguing for the motion.
Opposition: the side arguing against the motion.
Rebuttal: an answer that shows why the other side's argument does not hold.

name: Argue a motion in a debate
description: argue for or against a motion with prepared arguments, and rebut the other side's points on the spot.

name: Handle follow-up questions
description: answer follow-up questions in an academic conversation, such as an oral exam: expand on your answers, justify your views with examples, and say so honestly when you are unsure.

name: Narrator and point of view
description:
Narrator: the voice that tells the story, which is not the same as the author.
Point of view: whose eyes and thoughts the story is told through, from a first-person narrator to an omniscient one.
Unreliable narrator: a narrator whose account the reader has reason to doubt.

name: Characterisation
description:
Direct characterisation: the narrator tells the reader what a character is like.
Indirect characterisation: the reader works out what a character is like from what they say, do and think.
Round character: a complex character who develops during the story.
Flat character: a simple character built around one trait.

name: Theme, motif and symbol
description:
Theme: a central idea a text explores, such as power, identity or loss.
Motif: an image, idea or object that recurs and develops the theme.
Symbol: a concrete thing that also stands for something larger.

name: Irony
description:
Verbal irony: saying the opposite of what is meant.
Situational irony: an outcome that is the opposite of what was expected.
Dramatic irony: the reader or audience knows something a character does not.

name: Figurative language
description:
Simile: a comparison using like or as.
Metaphor: describing something by calling it something else.
Personification: giving human qualities to things, animals or nature.
Imagery: language that appeals to the senses.

name: Poetic devices
description:
Speaker: the voice in a poem, which is not necessarily the poet.
Stanza: a group of lines forming a unit in a poem.
Enjambment: a sentence running on from one line to the next without a pause.
Rhyme scheme: the pattern of rhymes at the ends of lines, written as letters such as ABAB.
Alliteration: the same sound at the start of several words close together.

name: Film techniques
description:
Shot size: how much of the scene the frame shows, from extreme long shot to close-up.
Camera angle: the position the camera films from, such as low angle or high angle.
Editing: how shots are cut and put together, which controls pace and connections.
Diegetic sound: sound that belongs to the world of the film, such as dialogue.
Non-diegetic sound: sound added for the audience, such as background music.

name: Analyse a short story
description: analyse how a short story creates meaning through its narrator, characters, setting, structure and literary devices.

name: Analyse a poem
description: analyse how a poem creates meaning through its speaker, imagery, sound and form, and connect the devices to what the poem is about.

name: Analyse a film scene
description: analyse how a film scene uses shot size, camera angle, editing, sound and acting to create mood and meaning.

name: Use quotations as evidence about literature
description: use short quotations, worked into your own sentences, as evidence when writing about literature, and comment on the words you quote.

name: Argue for an interpretation
description: argue for an interpretation of a literary text, support it with evidence from the text, and consider another possible reading.

name: Present a work you have chosen yourself
description: choose a novel, play or film yourself, and present and interpret it, explaining why you chose it and what it says about its themes.

name: Compare two works on the same theme
description: compare how two literary works or films treat the same theme, and explain what the comparison shows.

name: Write a literary essay
description: write an essay that interprets a literary text or film, organised around your reading of it and supported with quotations and analysis.

name: Standard English, dialect and accent
description:
Standard English: the variety used in education, news and official writing, with largely the same grammar and spelling everywhere.
Dialect: a regional or social variety with its own vocabulary and grammar.
Accent: the way a variety is pronounced.

name: RP and General American
description:
Received Pronunciation (RP): the accent traditionally regarded as standard in England, not tied to one region.
General American: the broad accent of much of the USA without strong regional features.
Rhotic accent: an accent where an r after a vowel is pronounced, as in most American English; RP is non-rhotic.

name: Kachru's three circles
description:
Inner circle: countries where English is the main first language, such as the UK, the USA and Australia.
Outer circle: countries where English is an official or second language because of colonial history, such as India, Nigeria and Singapore.
Expanding circle: countries where English is learned as a foreign language, such as Norway, Brazil and China.

name: Pidgin and creole
description:
Pidgin: a simplified contact language that arises when groups without a common language need to communicate, and that is nobody's first language.
Creole: a full language that develops when a pidgin becomes the first language of a community, such as Jamaican Creole.

name: Prestige and code-switching
description:
Linguistic prestige: the status a variety has in a society, which reflects the status of its speakers rather than the quality of the language.
Code-switching: shifting between languages or varieties depending on the situation and the people you are with.

name: British and American words
description:
flat (BrE): apartment (AmE)
lorry (BrE): truck (AmE)
pavement (BrE): sidewalk (AmE)
autumn (BrE): fall (AmE)
queue (BrE): line (AmE)
mobile phone (BrE): cell phone (AmE)
petrol (BrE): gas (AmE)
holiday (BrE): vacation (AmE)
rubbish (BrE): trash or garbage (AmE)
colour, centre, travelled (BrE): color, center, traveled (AmE)

name: Recognise varieties of English
description: recognise some major varieties of English when you hear or read them, such as British, American, Australian, Irish, Scottish, Indian and Nigerian English, and point to features that identify them.

name: Compare two varieties of English
description: describe differences in pronunciation, vocabulary, spelling and grammar between two varieties of English, with examples, and keep to one variety in your own writing.

name: Reflect on varieties and identity
description: reflect on why some varieties of English have higher status than others, and on how a variety can express identity, history and belonging.

name: Lingua franca
description: Lingua franca: a shared language used between people with different first languages, as English is in much of business, science, aviation and the internet.

name: Explain how English became a global language
description: explain how English became a global language through British colonialism, the economic and cultural power of the USA after 1945, and its role in science, technology and the internet.

name: Linguistic imperialism and domain loss
description:
Linguistic imperialism: the view that the spread of English pushes other languages and cultures aside and favours native speakers.
Domain loss: when a language stops being used in an area of society, such as Norwegian in research or parts of business.

name: Anglicism
description: Anglicism: an English word, phrase or structure taken into another language, such as deadline or å google in Norwegian.

name: Reflect on English influence on Norwegian
description: reflect on how English influences Norwegian, with examples from vocabulary, everyday speech and areas such as research and business, and discuss whether it is a threat or an enrichment.

name: Discuss English as a global language
description: discuss the advantages and disadvantages of English as a global language for exchanging information and opinions, including for people who do not speak it.

name: Echo chamber and filter bubble
description:
Echo chamber: an environment where people mostly meet opinions that confirm their own.
Filter bubble: the narrowing of what a user sees online by algorithms that build on their earlier behaviour.

name: Analyse how opinions spread online
description: analyse how information and opinions spread in English online, through social media, influencers and algorithms, and what this means for how people form their views.

name: Communicate with speakers of other first languages
description: adapt your English when communicating with people who speak it as a second language: avoid local idioms and slang, speak clearly, and check understanding without being condescending.

name: Polarisation
description: Polarisation: the movement of opinion in a society towards two opposing camps with little common ground.

name: Constitutional amendments in US debates
description:
First Amendment: freedom of religion, speech, the press, assembly and petition
Second Amendment: the right to keep and bear arms
Fourteenth Amendment: citizenship and equal protection of the laws
Nineteenth Amendment: women's right to vote

name: Reconciliation with Indigenous peoples
description: Reconciliation: the process of acknowledging and making amends for past wrongs against Indigenous peoples, such as the residential schools in Canada and the Stolen Generations in Australia.

name: Map a current debate
description: map a current social debate in an English-speaking country: the main positions, the groups that hold them, and their strongest arguments.

name: Explain the background of a debate
description: explain the historical background of a current debate, such as gun control in the USA, Indigenous rights in Canada or Australia, or immigration in the UK, and how that background shapes the debate today.

name: Compare how the media cover a debate
description: compare how two news outlets with different political leanings cover the same issue, and explain the differences in framing.

name: Compare a debate with Norway
description: compare a debate in an English-speaking country with a similar debate in Norway, and explain the differences through history, institutions or values.

name: Discuss a current debate independently
description: discuss a current social debate in an English-speaking country with independent reflection: weigh the arguments, question the assumptions on all sides, and reach and justify a view of your own.

name: Research question
description: Research question: a precise, open question that a project sets out to answer, narrow enough to be answered with the time and sources available.

name: Narrow a topic to a research question
description: choose a topic related to language, culture, society or science, and narrow it to a research question that can be answered.

name: Plan an in-depth project
description: plan an in-depth project: set a timeline, decide which kinds of sources to search, and record notes and references as you go.

name: Present an in-depth project
description: present the findings of your in-depth project orally or in writing, using English sources critically, and say where the sources disagree and what remains uncertain.
